To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ICOS costimulation requires IL-2 and that CTLA- 4 engagement prevents ICOS costimulation.
CTLA- 4 engagement prevents ICOS costimulation and this blockage is overcome by IL-2.
CTLA- 4 engagement prevents ICOS costimulation and IL-2 is required for sustained T cell proliferation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of T cell costimulation and the role that CTLA- 4 plays in the process.
the relationship between ICAM-1 and LFA-1 in the immune response and the mechanisms by which ICAM-1 regulates T cell activation.
the role of ICOS in T cell activation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ICOS-IL-2 costimulatory pathway is a critical component of the T cell immune response.

CTLA- 4 engagement prevents ICOS costimulation through an indirect mechanism by interfering with the signals needed for ICOS cell surface induction and through a direct mechanism by interfering with downstream signaling pathways that lead to the induction of IL- 2, IL-4, and IFNγ.

CTLA- 4 ligation blocks costimulation by ICOS by interfering with the signals needed for ICOS surface expression on resting T cells and by inhibiting ICOS-induced IL-2 production and IL-2-induced ICOS costimulation on activated T cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ICOS costimulatory signal is required for optimal IL-2 production and that CTLA- 4 engagement prevents ICOS costimulation, but that IL-2 can overcome this blockade.
ICOS costimulation requires IL-2 and is prevented by CTLA- 4 engagement.
the ICOS costimulatory pathway requires IL-2 and can be prevented by CTLA-2.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ICOS costimulation requires both IL-2 and CTLA-4 blockade.
ICOS and CTLA-4 are in direct competition for IL-2.
the ICOS costimulatory receptor is not a “free ride” and that ICOS signaling is carefully controlled.
